sections.summary: Paul introduces the topic of spiritual things or spiritual people with the formula 'now concerning,' indicating he is responding to a question from the Corinthians' letter.

sections.section_title: From Mute Idols to the Criterion of Confession
sections.summary: Paul contrasts the Corinthians' former pagan experience of being 'led astray to mute idols' with the present criterion of genuine Spirit inspiration: no one speaking by the Spirit says 'Jesus is cursed,' and no one can say 'Jesus is Lord' except by the Holy Spirit.

sections.section_title: One Source, Three Dimensions of Diversity
sections.summary: Paul establishes that the diversity of gifts, ministries, and workings all originate from the same Spirit, the same Lord, and the same God, establishing unity within diversity as the theological foundation.

sections.section_title: The Common Good as Governing Criterion
sections.summary: Paul states that to each person the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good, establishing benefit to the community as the purpose of all spiritual gifts.
Paul lists nine manifestations of the Spirit — wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues, and interpretation — all given through the one Spirit.
Paul emphasizes that the one and the same Spirit distributes gifts to each person individually as the Spirit wills, grounding the diversity in divine sovereignty rather than human merit.

sections.section_title: The Body Metaphor and the Baptism into One Body
sections.summary: Paul introduces the body metaphor — one body with many members — and grounds it in the community's shared experience of baptism into one body by one Spirit, whether Jew or Greek, slave or free, and being made to drink of one Spirit.

sections.section_title: The Body Cannot Reject Its Own Members
sections.summary: Paul argues through the personified body that no member can exclude itself by claiming it does not belong — the foot cannot say 'because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body' — because God arranged the members as he chose.

sections.section_title: The Body Cannot Despise Its Members
sections.summary: Paul argues the reverse: no member can dismiss another as unnecessary — the eye cannot say to the hand 'I have no need of you' — because the seemingly weaker and less honorable members are indispensable, and God has composed the body to give greater honor to the lesser.
Paul declares the community's identity: 'you are the body of Christ and individually members of it,' applying the entire body metaphor directly to the Corinthian assembly.

Paul lists God's ordered appointments in the assembly — apostles, prophets, teachers, then miracles, gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and kinds of tongues — with the hierarchical numbering emphasizing divine design.

Paul asks seven rhetorical questions ('Are all apostles? Are all prophets?'), each expecting 'no,' reinforcing that diversity of function is by divine design and no single gift belongs to every member.

sections.section_title: Transition to a Still More Excellent Way
sections.summary: Paul exhorts the community to earnestly desire the greater gifts and promises to show them a still more excellent way, setting up the transition to the love chapter.
